# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. Both tools offer features such as messaging, file sharing, and integrations, making them ideal for teams looking to improve collaboration and productivity. The core use case for both tools is team communication, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges a per-user fee.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to have full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up, while Slack is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Slack is more scalable and can handle larger teams, while Element may require more maintenance as the team grows.
* Feature difference: Element has end-to-end encryption, while Slack does not have this feature by default.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Large user base and community
* Many integrations available
* Scalable and reliable
* Limited control over data
### Element
* Free and self-hosted
* Full control over data
* End-to-end encryption
* Customizable and flexible
* Limited user base and community

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for large teams that need a scalable and reliable communication platform. It is also a good option for teams that are already familiar with the platform and have invested in integrations and customizations. On the other hand, Element is a good choice for teams that value data ownership and security. It is also a good option for small to medium-sized teams that are looking for a free and customizable communication platform.
Element is ideal for teams that require a high level of control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining the platform. It is also a good choice for teams that are looking for a platform with end-to-end encryption and are willing to trade off some ease of use for increased security.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which exports data in a JSON format.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it to your needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into Element.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and customizations in Element.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires a high level of technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element's scalability is limited compared to Slack, and may require more maintenance as the team grows. However, for teams that value data ownership and security, Element is a good choice, and we recommend switching to Element if you are a small to medium-sized team that is looking for a free and customizable communication platform.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need a high level of scalability
* Teams that value data ownership and security
* Teams that are looking for a free and customizable communication platform
* Teams that do not need a large number of integrations
* Teams that are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining the platform

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element requires more technical expertise to set up and use.
### Can I import my Slack data into Element?
Yes, you can use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into Element.
### Is Element more secure than Slack?
Yes, Element has end-to-end encryption, which makes it more secure than Slack.
### Can I use Element for large teams?
Not yet, Element's scalability is limited compared to Slack.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for teams, offering features such as chat, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those valuing data ownership and customizability. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and a key reason to switch might be the desire for self-hosting and cost savings.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own data, whereas Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack has a simpler setup process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms can scale to meet the needs of large teams, but Mattermost's self-hosted option provides more control.
* Feature difference: Mattermost offers more extensive customization options, including the ability to create custom integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations available
* Strong mobile app support
* Good customer support
* Limited customization options
### Mattermost
* Self-hosted option for data ownership and control
* Highly customizable
* Free, open-source option
* Scalable and secure
* Steeper learning curve due to customization options

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations. It's suitable for small to medium-sized teams that don't require extensive customization. Mattermost, on the other hand, is ideal for teams that value data ownership, customizability, and self-hosting. It's a good fit for larger teams or organizations with specific security and compliance requirements.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either self-hosted or using a cloud provider.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to import your Slack data, which supports JSON format.
4. Configure your Mattermost instance, including setting up users, channels, and integrations.
5. Test your Mattermost instance to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready alternative to Slack, offering a robust set of features and a high degree of customizability. However, one technical limitation to consider is the potential complexity of setting up and managing a self-hosted Mattermost instance, which may require significant technical expertise. For teams that value data ownership and customizability, Mattermost is a clear choice, but teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations may find Slack a better fit.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need extensive integrations
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that value data ownership and customizability
* Large teams (over 50 users) that require self-hosting for security and compliance
* Teams that don't need mobile app support
* Teams that prioritize cost savings over ease of use

## FAQ
### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, as well as a paid, cloud-hosted option. The self-hosted option is free, but teams will need to cover server costs.
### Can I use Mattermost with my existing Slack integrations?

### Is Mattermost as easy to use as Slack?
Mattermost has a steeper learning curve due to its customization options, but it's still relatively easy to use.
### Can I import my Slack data into Mattermost?

### Is Mattermost suitable for small teams?

| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### GitLab

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [gitlabhq/gitlabhq](https://github.com/gitlabhq/gitlabhq) * ~24k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub suits open-source projects wanting maximum community visibility or teams deeply integrated with GitHub Actions workflows.

**Choose GitLab if:** GitLab self-hosted is ideal for enterprises needing full control over their DevOps stack or regulated industries.

## Migration Path

GitLab provides a GitHub importer that migrates repositories, issues, PRs, wikis, and milestones. Update CI configuration from GitHub Actions to GitLab CI/CD YAML format.

## Our Take

GitLab is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your GitLab instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted GitLab will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is GitLab free to use?
Yes. GitLab is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to GitLab?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the GitLab import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does GitLab get regular updates?
Yes. GitLab has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use GitLab without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if GitLab development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [GitLab](https://gitlab.com) before making decisions.*

title: Figma vs Penpot
comparison_markdown:
# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are both design and prototyping tools used by product teams, designers, and developers to create user interfaces and user experiences. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering switching from Figma to Penpot, particularly due to Penpot's free and self-hosted options. The core use case for both tools is collaborative design, and a key reason someone would switch is to reduce costs or gain more control over their design data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma has a per-user monthly fee, while Penpot is free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Penpot allows full data ownership, whereas Figma stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Penpot requires more technical setup, especially for self-hosting, whereas Figma is cloud-based and easily accessible.
* Scalability: Figma is designed for large-scale teams and enterprises, while Penpot is more suitable for smaller teams or individuals.
* Integration difference: Figma has a more extensive library of third-party plugins and integrations, while Penpot has limited but growing support for external tools.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Pros:
  + Easy to use and collaborate
  + Large community and extensive plugin library
  + Scalable for large teams
  + Cloud-based for easy access
  + Regular updates with new features
* Cons:
  + Expensive for large teams
  + Limited data ownership and control
  + Dependence on Figma's servers for data storage
### Penpot
* Pros:
  + Free and open-source
  + Full data ownership and control
  + Self-hosting option for security and customization
  + Growing community and improving features
  + Customizable and extensible
* Cons:
  + Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements
  + Limited plugin library and integrations
  + Smaller community compared to Figma
  + May require technical expertise for setup and maintenance
  + Limited support for large-scale teams

## When to Choose Each
Figma is suitable for large teams, enterprises, or those who prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations. It's ideal for teams that don't mind paying a premium for a cloud-based solution and have limited technical expertise. On the other hand, Penpot is perfect for smaller teams, individuals, or those who value data ownership and control. It's also suitable for teams with technical expertise who can handle self-hosting and customization.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to upload your designs.
3. Review and adjust your designs to ensure compatibility with Penpot.
4. Invite your team to collaborate on Penpot and set up self-hosting if necessary.
5. Explore Penpot's features and plugins to enhance your design workflow.

## Our Take
Penpot is not yet production-ready for most users due to its limited plugin library and smaller community. However, it shows great promise for teams that value data ownership and control. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is Penpot's current lack of support for real-time collaboration, which may hinder large-scale team workflows. We recommend switching to Penpot if you're a small team or individual with technical expertise, but for larger teams or those who rely on Figma's extensive plugin library, it's best to stick with Figma.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need extensive integrations
* Individuals who value data ownership and control
* Teams with technical expertise who can handle self-hosting
* Those who prioritize cost savings over ease of use
* Designers who don't require real-time collaboration features

## FAQ
### Is Penpot completely free?
Yes, Penpot is free and open-source, with no costs per user.
### Can I self-host Penpot?
Yes, Penpot offers self-hosting options for added security and customization.
### Does Penpot support real-time collaboration?
Not yet, but the feature is in development and expected to be released soon.
### Is Penpot suitable for large teams?
No, Penpot is currently more suitable for smaller teams or individuals due to its limited plugin library and scalability.
### Can I import my Figma designs into Penpot?
Yes, Penpot offers an import tool that supports Figma design files.
